intro: Dear Reviewer, thank you for your questions.
closing: We hope these answers warrant reassessing the score.

fragments.text: As submitted, none fully: Theorem 5 needs gradient-scaled or constant steps, but our runs anneal by cosine. Since submission, we have bounds for both EF21 methods under constant and cosine rates with fixed momentum; they cover Tables 1–2 up to the Newton–Schulz approximation, but not Table 3 (momentum warmup). We will add this as a table.
fragments.notes:
Evidence: T1: submitted supplement A.10; aaai_article/ef21_nesterov_convergence.tex, ef21_fixed_radius.tex, ef21_rate_takeaways.tex. Gradient-scaled steps and horizon-tuned momentum for the separate squared-moment result; never infer it by squaring a first moment. T1/G1: aaai_article/ef21_fixed_radius.tex (explicit separability step), ef21_nesterov_convergence.tex, and signmuon_addendum_body.tex (conditional SignMuon theorem and open EF21 cross-layer target). J1: separate candidate derivation in evidence/EF21_JOINT_SMOOTHNESS.md; not a revised-manuscript result and not relied on by the replies. F1: lean_proofs/README.md, PAPER_AUDIT.md, comparator/VERIFICATION.json (45 statements, passed 2026-10-23; reference and dependency hashes rechecked), and research/nesterov/lean-verification.log. Original ascent/output-EF divergence results and the generalized EF21 tracking/convergence arguments have Lean proofs. The printed cosine-sum specialization is a manual composition. The added conditional plain SignMuon theorem and softplus extensions are not claimed Lean-verified.
Finding / complete answer: We generalized the EF21 analysis to EMA/Nesterov and deterministic learning rates. Its tracking and convergence arguments are formalized in Lean. Constant/cosine corollaries follow by schedule specialization, whose printed cosine sum is not itself a complete exported Lean theorem. Approximate directions are admitted through explicit error/quality assumptions. The squared-gradient rate still needs gradient-dependent steps and the manuscript retains separability.

Revision 10: the printed fixed-radius/constant-cosine theorem assumes exact polar factors. Its tracking budget separates initialization, movement and noise, with compressor constants. The more general Lean BlockTrajectory.Oracle assumes a spectral-radius bound and <h,D_t(h)> >= gain*||h||_* - delta_t, and expected_stationarity_sum adds sum_t eta_t*delta_t (summed over blocks), normalized by mass in expected_stationarity. This condition exposes approximation loss; it does not certify delta_t for the implemented solver. Earlier notes saying numerical accuracy is quantified must be read with this distinction.

fragments.text: SignMuon itself is concurrent: Mishra et al. is a May 2026 preprint developed independently. The EF21 rates are inherited; Theorems 1–4 are our contribution.
fragments.notes:
Evidence: P1: Gruntkowska et al. 2025 EF21-Muon, Algorithm 3 / Theorem 19 / Remark 23; Modoranu et al. ICML 2024; Mishra et al. SignMuon v2 (17 October 2026), Section 4 / Appendix F. The current main article comparison to Mishra v1 is stale and must be replaced. N1: submitted Theorems 1–4 and proofs; aaai_article/ef21_signmuon_divergence.tex; evidence/verified_claims.json exact rational ascent/cycle certificates. Theorem 4 objective depends on fixed eta and mu; no decreasing-schedule impossibility follows. F1: lean_proofs/README.md, PAPER_AUDIT.md, comparator/VERIFICATION.json (45 statements, passed 2026-10-23; reference and dependency hashes rechecked), and research/nesterov/lean-verification.log. Original ascent/output-EF divergence results and the generalized EF21 tracking/convergence arguments have Lean proofs. The printed cosine-sum specialization is a manual composition. The added conditional plain SignMuon theorem and softplus extensions are not claimed Lean-verified.
Finding / complete answer: Practical SignMuon and the general EF21 framework are prior/concurrent work. Our supported contribution is the controlled comparison of six placements/EF variants, strong sign-based performance and distinct sign/polar failure mechanisms. Mishra v2 has conditional actual-vote stochastic momentum theory; the current manuscript’s v1-only comparison must be updated. The added conditional SignMuon theorem is new to this submission, not claimed as the first conditional SignMuon result.

fragments.text: You are right: nanoGPT averages full-precision gradients before compressing, so it tests centralized optimizers; Sec. 5.3 will say so. Distributed compression is tested on federated CNN2, where we added heterogeneous clients: even at this scale, SignMuon falls from 85.7% to 43.0%, while the guaranteed EF21 methods keep 84% (our response to 7S1b, Q2).
fragments.notes:
Evidence: E3: submitted Table 3 and supplement A.16–A.17; code/results/nanogpt/runs.csv, diagnostics.csv, SUMMARY.md; one independent unpinned run per compressed method, full-precision gradient reduce-scatter before optimizer.
Finding / complete answer: The reviewer is correct. Full-precision gradient averaging precedes the owning-rank optimizer; parameter all-gather follows. Local compress-then-vote semantics and actual one-bit communication gains are not tested by this experiment.

reply_topics.heading: 1. Re guarantee coverage:
reply_topics.question: Appendix A.10 states that the squared-gradient guarantee requires the learning-rate rule $\eta_{t,i}=\gamma_i\|g_{t,i}\|_*$, which is not used in the experiments. It also states that the experimental EF21-MuonSign schedule is not covered by either corollary, and that the Nesterov variant used in nanoGPT is outside the theoretical framework. Could the authors clarify which guarantees, if any, apply to each EF21 experiment in Tables 1–3? Currently, the paper compares methods with theoretical guarantees, but the actual experimental configurations do not necessarily satisfy their assumptions. This should be made clear in the main text.

reply_topics.heading: 2. Re Table 2:
reply_topics.question: I noticed some values differ between tables that appear to describe the same experiments. Federated MuonSign achieves $80.68\pm1.88$ in Table 2 but $82.94\pm0.19$ under the unit-gain rule in Table A8, whose caption refers to the same five seeds as Table 2. With the Table A8 value, MuonSign is above SignSGD rather than below it, which changes the ordering stated in Section 5.2. Could the authors explain these values and state which runs support the main conclusions?

reply_topics.heading: 3. Re our contribution:
reply_topics.question: The most interesting finding is that sign-after methods consistently perform best, despite being the ones targeted by the negative theoretical results. Even the random quadratic experiments show positive alignment between SignMuon's update and the gradient. This raises a more important question than whether the method can fail on carefully constructed examples: under what reasonable assumptions does sign compression after orthogonalization preserve a useful descent direction, and why are the theoretical failure cases not observed in practice? Appendix A.7 already identifies the gradient-weighted sign disagreement term that could serve as a starting point for such an analysis, but the paper does not pursue it. Instead, the theory focuses on worst-case counterexamples, while the positive convergence results largely follow from existing work. Moreover, SignMuon and its practical effectiveness have already been reported in the concurrent work cited by the authors, so these cannot be considered new contributions.

reply_topics.heading: 4. Re nanoGPT:
reply_topics.question: The nanoGPT experiments do not actually evaluate the proposed distributed compression methods. As explained in Appendix A.16, the gradients are first averaged in full precision using reduce-scatter, and the compressed update is then applied locally. In contrast, Algorithms A8–A9 compress each worker's updates before aggregation. This is an important difference, since averaging the signs of local polar factors is generally not equivalent to taking the sign of the polar factor after averaging. Although Appendix A.16 describes this implementation, Section 5.3 presents the results as evidence that the one-bit methods work for language modeling without clearly explaining this distinction. The experiments therefore only support the centralized variants and do not demonstrate the performance or communication benefits of the proposed distributed methods at this scale.

reply_topics.heading: 5. Re presentation:
reply_topics.question: Throughout the paper, important explanations are deferred to appendix sections (A.7, A.10, A.12, A.16, A.17), and several figure captions are unnecessarily long. Overall, the paper needs a much simpler and more direct presentation, particularly in the sections explaining the main results, ideally with a table stating which implementation choices each theorem covers.
